title: Everest is the highest peak, but not the tallest or farthest out
body: Mount Everest’s summit, 8,849 m above sea level, is the highest point on Earth measured from sea level. But Earth bulges at the equator, so Ecuador’s Chimborazo, only 6,263 m high, has a summit about 2 km farther from Earth’s centre, the farthest point on the surface from the core. And measured from its base on the seafloor, Hawaii’s Mauna Kea is taller than Everest.

slides.heading: The bulge
slides.text: Earth’s spin flattens it slightly: the equatorial radius is about 21 km larger than the polar radius. Peaks near the equator get a free boost.

slides.heading: Mauna Kea’s hidden half
slides.text: Mauna Kea rises 4,207 m above sea level, but most of it is underwater. From its seafloor base it rises roughly 9 to 10 km, depending on how the base is defined.

slides.heading: Three different records
slides.text: Highest above sea level: Everest. Tallest from base to peak: Mauna Kea. Farthest from Earth’s centre: Chimborazo.

slides.question: Why is Chimborazo’s summit farther from Earth’s centre than Everest’s?
options: Sea level is lower near the equator
slides.explanation: Earth’s spin flattens it: the equatorial radius is about 21 km larger than the polar one, so Chimborazo, near the equator, ends up about 2 km farther out than Everest.
